theme_intro: This last week is about getting help, and about what the research honestly says help can do. We look at what a first appointment is like, what talking therapies and medication actually do, what happens when the first treatment does not work, and how to build a plan for the road ahead. None of it replaces what you have already practised; it adds to it.

days.title: Asking for help is treatment
days.quote: The occurrence of depression does not mean that the person is weak or lazy.
days.quote_source: World Health Organization (2016), mhGAP Intervention Guide
days.explanation:
You have kept showing up for eleven weeks. Today is about one more step, the one many people put off for months: telling a doctor.

The World Health Organization trains health workers around the world with a guide called mhGAP. Its first messages for a person with depression are blunt. Depression is very common and can happen to anybody. Having it does not mean you are weak or lazy. People say ‘pull yourself together’ because they cannot see it the way they see a broken arm. And the harsh, hopeless views depression gives you about yourself are likely to lift once the depression lifts. That is a medical statement, not a pep talk.

A first appointment is plainer than you fear. The doctor will ask how long you have felt low or lost interest (two weeks or more matters), about sleep, appetite, energy, concentration, guilt and hopeless thoughts, and whether you have thought about harming yourself. They may check for physical causes such as thyroid problems or anaemia. Then you decide together: support and daily structure, a talking therapy, medication, or a combination, with a second visit within a week or two.

You do not need the right words. Here is a script: ‘For several weeks I have felt low most days and stopped enjoying things. I am not sleeping well and I am struggling to function. I think I may be depressed, and I would like help.’ If you are thinking about ending your life, please call a crisis line today; the Help page has your country’s number.
days.challenge: Copy today’s script into the notes app on your phone and edit it until every sentence is true for you. Then find your doctor’s phone number or online booking page and save it next to the script, so that making the call is one tap away. If you already see a doctor or therapist, write down one thing you have not yet told them. If even that is too much today, answer one question in writing: ‘How does my life change when I am depressed?’
reflection_questions: What has kept you from asking for help so far, and how much of that is the depression talking?
Who in your life would be relieved to hear you had made an appointment?
If a friend described your last month to you as their own, what would you tell them to do?

scripture.text: Those who are healthy have no need for a physician, but those who are sick.

days.title: What talking therapy actually does
days.quote: The aim of cognitive therapy is to help individuals realise that they can influence their mood by identifying and changing their thoughts and beliefs.
days.quote_source: Nathan, Rees, Lim & Correia (2003), Back from the Bluez
days.explanation:
‘Talking therapy’ can sound like paying someone to listen while you cry. The therapies with the best evidence for depression are more practical than that, and you have already tasted them in this programme.

Cognitive therapy starts from an observation made by the Centre for Clinical Interventions: depressed people think very negative thoughts about themselves, their lives and their future, and this worsens their mood. In therapy you learn to catch those thoughts, weigh the evidence and build more balanced ones. It is structured, time-limited and focused on the here and now. Behavioural activation is its partner: scheduling small activities, solving problems step by step, acting before motivation arrives. Interpersonal therapy works on the relationships around the depression. It names four common triggers, grief, disputes, life changes and loneliness, and helps you work on one or two of them.

You do not need a specialist in a private office for this to work. In 2016 a trial in Peshawar, Pakistan, gave 346 distressed adults five weekly sessions of problem solving, activity scheduling and social support, delivered by local health workers with no previous clinical training. Three months later their depression scores averaged about 6 on a 21-point scale, compared with about 9 for people who saw only their doctor. The WHO now trains community workers to run eight-session interpersonal therapy groups, and in 2015 its guideline panel concluded that for moderate-to-severe depression talking therapy and medication are both reasonable first choices; for mild depression, therapy comes first.

A counsellor, a group, a properly trained church-based programme: these count.
days.challenge: Spend 10 minutes finding out what talking-therapy options exist where you live: ask your doctor’s receptionist, search your health insurer’s or national health service’s website, or ask one person you know who has had therapy. Write down one concrete option with a phone number or link. If that is too much today, write the four interpersonal therapy triggers on a piece of paper, grief, dispute, life change, loneliness, and circle the one that fits your last year best. Keep the paper for your first appointment.
reflection_questions: Which of the four triggers, grief, a dispute, a life change or loneliness, has been closest to your own low mood?
What would you want a therapist to understand about you in the first ten minutes?
Which of the small practices from the last eleven weeks already felt like a kind of therapy?

scripture.text: Where there is no counsel, plans fail; but in a multitude of counselors they are established.

days.title: Medication, honestly
days.quote: Medications should never be stopped just because the person experiences some improvement.
days.quote_source: World Health Organization (2016), mhGAP Intervention Guide
days.explanation:
Here is the antidepressant debate, honestly.

In 2008 Irving Kirsch and colleagues obtained every trial that drug companies had sent to the US regulator for four antidepressants, published or not: 35 trials, about 5,000 people. On the standard depression scale, people on the drug improved by about 9.6 points and people on a dummy pill by about 7.8. Both groups got much better. The gap between them was small, and widened only as depression became severe. In 2010 Fournier and colleagues pooled patient-level data from six trials and found the same shape: little or no added benefit in mild-to-moderate depression, a substantial benefit in very severe depression.

Others pushed back. Penn and Tracy note that a re-analysis of the same data found a larger gap, that averages hide the many people who respond to one drug and not another, and that staying on medication after recovery cut relapse risk by about 70 percent. Kirsch would reserve the pills for the most severe cases; the WHO and most national guidelines instead keep medication and talking therapy as equal first-line options for moderate and severe depression, with therapy, activity and support coming first in mild depression.

Three facts matter more than the argument. Antidepressants are not addictive. They usually take several weeks to work. And they must never be stopped suddenly or because you feel a bit better; the WHO advises continuing for nine to twelve months after you are well. If you take medication and have doubts, bring them to your doctor.
days.challenge: Write down two questions for your doctor about medication, whether you take it or not. ‘How long before I should expect to notice anything?’ ‘What do I do if I get side effects in the first days?’ ‘Once I feel well, how long would I stay on it, and how would we come off it together?’ Keep the questions for your next appointment. If you take medication, check tonight that tomorrow’s dose is ready. If that is too much, tell one person which of today’s three facts surprised you.
reflection_questions: What have you heard about antidepressants from family, friends or church, and how does it sit beside what the studies actually found?
If you take medication, what would help you take it every day as prescribed? If you do not, what would you want to ask before deciding?
Where does hope come from for you: a pill, a person, a practice, a prayer, or several at once?

scripture.text: He came to him, and bound up his wounds, pouring on oil and wine. He set him on his own animal, brought him to an inn, and took care of him.

days.title: When the first treatment does not work
days.quote: It is clear that continued active, rationalized and individually optimized treatment does work for many.
days.explanation:
If the first thing you tried did not work, you are in the majority, and that is not the end of the story.

The largest real-world study of depression treatment, STAR*D, followed 3,671 adults. After that first step, about 37 percent were in remission, meaning nearly symptom-free. Those who were not moved to a second step: switching to a different medication, adding a second one, or adding cognitive therapy. About 31 percent of them remitted. Third and fourth steps helped fewer, around 13 percent each. Added together, roughly two in three people reached remission over the four steps. Remission took five to seven weeks per step, and people who needed more steps relapsed more often in the following year.

Two lessons: ‘the first one did not work’ is common and the next step has a real chance; and it takes weeks, not days, to know.

For people who have tried several medications there are further options. Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) uses a magnetic coil held against the scalp in daily sessions for three to six weeks. In 307 patients who had not improved on an average of two and a half medications, 58 percent responded and 37 percent remitted; a year later about six in ten of the responders had kept the benefit. In controlled trials TMS is roughly twice as effective as a sham coil.

None of this is yours to arrange alone. It is a list of questions for your doctor, and permission not to give up after one try.
days.challenge: If you are in treatment and it does not seem to be helping, write down today: when you started, what has changed even slightly, and what has not. Take that note to your next appointment and ask: ‘What is our next step if this is not enough?’ If you are not in treatment, write down one treatment you had assumed was not for you, and one question about it. If that is too much, rate your mood from 0 to 10 and date it, to compare in a month.
reflection_questions: When something has not worked before, what did you tell yourself about it, and about yourself?
What would ‘a little better’ look like for you, concretely, four weeks from now?
Who could help you keep asking about next steps in the weeks when you have no energy to ask?

scripture.text: Wait for Yahweh. Be strong, and let your heart take courage. Yes, wait for Yahweh.

days.title: Building your care team
days.quote: Often, problems seem bigger than they really are when a person tries to deal with them on their own.
days.quote_source: Nathan, Rees, Lim & Correia (2003), Back from the Bluez
days.explanation:
Nobody recovers from depression alone, and no one expects you to.

The WHO’s guide for health workers describes care for depression as a set of roles, not a single rescuer. The doctor assesses, checks physical health, discusses medication if appropriate and keeps follow-up going: a second visit within a week, then regular contact through the first three months. A therapist or trained counsellor does the structured work on thoughts, activity and relationships. Family and carers are included with your consent, and the guide asks the health worker to help you reactivate your previous social network: the gatherings, neighbours and activities that used to hold you.

A review of depression care in low- and middle-income countries found that ‘collaborative care’, where a primary care team, a case manager and a supervising specialist share one patient, works, and that depression treatments are just as effective in disadvantaged settings. In Chile, stepped care for women with depression led to improvement at six months in about 70 percent, compared with 30 percent in usual care.

Non-professionals matter in a different way. The Centre for Clinical Interventions puts it plainly: find someone with whom you can sit down and have a good talk, not a therapy session, a chance to talk through what is going on. A friend or pastor is not your therapist and does not need to be. Their part is to listen, to walk alongside, perhaps to come with you to an appointment. Your part today is to see who is already on your team, and where the gaps are.
days.challenge: Draw a small table with four rows: Doctor, Therapist or counsellor, Friend or pastor, Family. Next to each write a name, or ‘none yet’. Choose one gap and one small move toward filling it: a booking, a message, a question to someone who might know. Make that move today if you can. If that is too much, write the name of one person who listened well in the past year and send them a two-line thank you.
reflection_questions: Who already carries part of this with you, even if you have never called them a team?
What have you expected one person to provide that is really several people’s roles?
What would make it easier to let a professional and a friend each do their own part?

scripture.text: Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labor. For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow; but woe to him who is alone when he falls, and doesn’t have another to lift him up.

days.title: Your early-warning plan
days.quote: Slip-ups in progress can happen at any time and are to be expected.
days.quote_source: Nathan, Rees, Lim & Correia (2003), Back from the Bluez
days.explanation:
Depression tends to come back. That is not a threat; it is the reason to make a plan now, while you can think clearly.

In STAR*D, people who had needed more treatment steps relapsed more often during the following year, and the researchers said this should be expected. The WHO guide asks health workers to keep seeing people until they have been free of symptoms for nine to twelve months and, if medication is part of the picture, to continue it over that period. Any change to medication belongs in a conversation with your doctor.

The Centre for Clinical Interventions ends its depression programme with a module on staying well. Three points. Expect slip-ups and down days, and refuse the trap of believing that a bad day means you are ‘back to square one’. Keep practising the strategies until they become habits. Keep a person to talk to. Its ‘Healthy Me’ worksheet lists the areas to watch: balanced thoughts, pleasant activities, social activities, exercise, relaxation, self-care, goals, social support.

A relapse plan has three parts. Early signs, yours specifically: for many people it is sleep changing, cancelling plans, dropping the small practices, or thoughts turning harsh. Actions: what helped most in these twelve weeks, written down so you do not have to remember while low. People: who to tell, and the doctor’s number. If your thoughts ever turn to ending your life, please call a crisis line that same day; the Help page has your country’s number.
days.challenge: Take one page and write three headings: My early signs, What helps me, Who I tell. Under the first, list three changes that came before your last low period. Under the second, list the three practices from this programme that helped most. Under the third, write two names and your doctor’s number. Photograph the page so it is on your phone. If that is too much, write only the three early signs today and finish the rest tomorrow.
reflection_questions: Looking back, what were the first small signs last time, weeks before you called it depression?
Which of this programme’s practices would you most regret losing, and what is most likely to make you drop it?
Who would you want to notice if you started slipping, and have you told them what to look for?

scripture.text: He brought me up also out of a horrible pit, out of the miry clay. He set my feet on a rock, and gave me a firm place to stand.

days.title: Three things to carry forward
days.quote: However, it is very important to keep this in mind: depression is treatable.
days.quote_source: World Health Organization & Columbia University (2016), Group Interpersonal Therapy for Depression
days.explanation:
Eighty-four days ago you opened the first message of this programme. Whatever state you are in today, you came back often enough to reach the last one. That matters.

The WHO’s therapy manual puts the central fact in one line: depression is treatable. The evidence behind that line is not a promise that everything resolves; it is a pattern. In the largest real-world study, roughly two in three people reached remission when they kept going through the treatment steps. Lay counsellors in a conflict-affected city eased depression with five sessions. When Irving Kirsch, the sharpest critic of antidepressants, pooled trials of medication, psychotherapy, their combination and exercise, he found no significant difference between them. Read that as hope: there is more than one road out, and the roads can be combined.

You have walked parts of many roads in these weeks: meeting your thoughts differently, moving, sleeping, eating, drinking water, going outside, easing off alcohol, giving thanks, reaching out, praying or resting, and now asking for help. The Centre for Clinical Interventions says the task after a programme is to keep practising a few things until they become habits, and that progress may be a bumpy road but a rewarding journey on the whole.

So choose three. Not twelve. The three that moved something for you, however slightly. Write them where you will see them. If you fall into the pit again, begin again at Day 1, and tell someone. Starting over is not failure. It is the plan.
days.challenge: Look back through your journal, or your memory of these twelve weeks, and pick three practices you will keep: one for your body, one for your mind, one that involves another person. Write each as a sentence with a when: ‘Walk ten minutes after breakfast.’ Put the list where you will see it every morning. Tell one person which three you chose. If that is too much today, choose one, and let it be the one that came easiest.
reflection_questions: Which week of this programme surprised you most, and why?
What do you know about your depression now that you did not know 84 days ago?
If someone you love were starting Day 1 tomorrow, what would you most want them to know?

scripture.text: It is because of Yahweh’s loving kindnesses that we are not consumed, because his compassion doesn’t fail. They are new every morning. Great is your faithfulness.
